extracted.intended_audience: essayists and cultivated readers of periodical essays (persons of taste and learning)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing short, public-facing moral and humorous essays (Spectator-style): how to condense, shape, and aim short sheets so each stands as a complete, instructive piece and resists party-driven scurrility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quintessence / concision
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Sheet should be a kind of Treatise, and make out in Thought what it wants in Bulk; an Essay-Writer must practise in the Chymical Method, and give the Virtue of a full Draught in a few Drops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distil larger ideas into concentrated, potent short pieces rather than sprawling paragraphs. Prefer the 'quintessence' of a subject: deliver the essential insight in brief, well-chosen material so a short paper reads like a complete treatise. Anti-patterns: bulky, diffuse writing; needless enlargements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-contained short-sheet
rubrics_metrics.description: It is often expected that every Sheet should be a kind of Treatise ... make out in Thought what it wants in Bulk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each issue/paper should treat its chosen point sufficiently that readers feel the piece is complete. Even if composed of broken hints or sketches, a sheet must have a clear, finished intellectual shape. Scoring note: completeness of thought over physical length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop the comic or satiric point fully
rubrics_metrics.description: That a Point of Humour should be worked up in all its Parts; and a Subject touched upon in its most essential Articles, without the Repetitions, Tautologies and Enlargements, that are indulged to longer Labours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the piece uses humour or satire, ensure the joke/point is developed through its parts so its effect is clear and satisfying. Avoid relying on repetition or padding to make a short joke seem longer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repetitions, tautologies, and enlargements
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects should be treated 'without the Repetitions, Tautologies and Enlargements, that are indulged to longer Labours.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prune redundant phrasing and circular reasoning. In short-form work, verbosity and tautological emphasis are defects. Editing should remove expansions that add bulk without adding thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the press to instruct and improve public morals
rubrics_metrics.description: Our common Prints would be of great Use were they thus calculated to diffuse good Sense through the Bulk of a People, to clear up their Understandings, animate their Minds with Virtue, dissipate the Sorrows of a heavy Heart, or unbend the Mind from its more severe Employments with innocent Amusements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim the content toward public improvement: instruct, clarify, cheer, and morally edify. The press's purpose should lean toward wisdom and virtue rather than mere partisan agitation or transient entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target an audience of persons of sense; accept some readers will be unreceptive
rubrics_metrics.description: The many Letters which come to me from Persons of the best Sense in both Sexes ... I am not at all mortified, when sometimes I see my Works thrown aside by Men of no Taste nor Learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write for an attentive, discerning readership rather than trying to please everyone. Recognize that some readers ('moles') are unreceptive due to ignorance or envy; this does not invalidate the essay's value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality and anti‑partisanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Honest Men of all Parties should enter into an Association ... this neutral Body should act with a Regard to nothing but Truth and Equity, and divest themselves of the little Heats and Prepossessions that cleave to Parties of all Kinds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid partisan bias in judgment and criticism. Evaluate works and persons by truth, equity, and merit rather than party affiliation. Anti-patterns: treating reputation or quality as contingent on political allegiance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject calumny and unproven scandal as foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one Piece of Sophistry practised by both Sides, ... taking any scandalous Story that has been ever whispered or invented of a Private Man, for a known undoubted Truth ... Calumnies that have been never proved, or have been often refuted, are the ordinary Postulatums of these infamous Scriblers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base assertions, satire, or moral judgments on rumour or unverified accusations. Maintain evidentiary care; avoid repeating or canonizing scandalous stories without proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value works on intrinsic merit, not party usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: We should then single every Criminal out of the Herd ... On the contrary, we should shelter distressed Innocence, and defend Virtue, however beset with Contempt or Ridicule, Envy or Defamation. ... We should not any longer regard our Fellow Subjects as Whigs or Tories, but should make the Man of Merit our Friend, and the Villain our Enemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise or reproach should follow the subject's qualities rather than the author's political usefulness. Resist rewarding incompetence because it serves a faction or punishing merit because it opposes one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve timelessness over transient fashion
rubrics_metrics.description: Great Masters in Painting never care for drawing People in the Fashion; as very well knowing that the Headdress ... that now prevails ... will make a very odd Figure, and perhaps look monstrous in the Eyes of Posterity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor durable, classical modes of expression or representation rather than slavish adherence to current fashions, which date works rapidly. In portraits and characterization, choose elements likely to age well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain, simple expression and allegiance to obvious truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed Form of an Association ... 'We do in our Consciences believe two and two make four; and that we shall adjudge any Man whatsoever to be our Enemy who endeavours to persuade us to the contrary.' ... 'It is our Resolution ... to call Black black, and White white.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commit to clear, unambiguous statements of fact and truth in public discourse. Satirical asides aside, this is a standard for plain-speaking and intellectual honesty: avoid deliberate equivocation or rhetorical obfuscation.
